slice_results.behavior_summary: At runtime, the code accesses and manipulates DOM elements and SVG graphics using the SVG.js library, handling user input events such as mouse and keyboard interactions. It reads image data from hardcoded or user-provided image URLs via standard HTML image loading, processes coordinate transformations, and manages internal data structures for shapes and labels. No network, file system, or system execution APIs are invoked, and no suspicious hardcoded IPs, URLs, or commands are present, resulting in no direct security impact.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a client-side JavaScript library for SVG-based image annotation and labeling. It primarily manipulates DOM elements, handles user input events (mouse and keyboard), and manages graphical shapes and labels. There is no evidence of obfuscation, code injection, remote script loading, environment manipulation, or data exfiltration. The code does not use eval, does not decode or execute payloads, and does not access system or network APIs beyond standard image loading. Compared to the known malicious patterns, it lacks any suspicious or malicious indicators such as embedded scripts in SVG, remote script injection, or system data collection and execution. The behavior is consistent with a legitimate UI component for image annotation.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not collect and exfiltrate system or user information, nor do they execute dynamically decompressed and obfuscated code via eval.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Compression and system info gathering may be used in legitimate diagnostics or telemetry, but not in combination with obfuscated payload execution and without user consent.

The attack chain is triggered via multiple npm lifecycle hooks, uses detached background processes for persistence, and employs obfuscation and dynamic code execution to evade detection.

It manages user input events and shape data purely in-memory without any network, file system, or system command interactions. Unlike the known malicious patterns, which involve SVG files containing embedded JavaScript leading to Stored XSS or SVG files with external DTD references causing SSRF, this code does not embed or execute arbitrary scripts from untrusted sources, nor does it parse or serve SVG files from external inputs. The code does not perform any sanitization or serve SVG files; it only creates and edits SVG elements programmatically within a controlled environment. There are no suspicious hardcoded IPs, URLs, or commands, and no evidence of data exfiltration or code injection. Therefore, it does not match the malicious patterns and is considered benign.

  <text x="5" y="15" fill="red">I♡XML!</text>
</svg>
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when the SVG file is parsed by the application, the parser processes the external DTD reference in the DOCTYPE declaration, causing the application to initiate an HTTP request to the specified host (e.g., localhost:2323), resulting in potential SSRF or DoS.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The SVG file includes an external DTD reference in the DOCTYPE declaration, which is unnecessary for standard SVG rendering and can force the application to make arbitrary network requests during parsing.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal SVG files do not require external DTDs and should not cause the application to initiate outbound network connections during image parsing.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: External DTDs may be used in rare, advanced, or legacy SVG workflows, but are not typical in standard or modern SVG files.
key_indicators: Presence of <!DOCTYPE ... SYSTEM ...> in SVG files submitted by users
Outbound network requests triggered during SVG parsing
HTTP requests to internal or non-standard hosts (e.g., localhost, internal IPs) initiated by image processing components
Unusual User-Agent strings (e.g., Java/1.7.0_60-ea) in network requests originating from SVG parsing

package_info.why_malicious: Apache Batik is vulnerable to XML External Entity (XXE) attacks when parsing SVG files. This allows attackers to craft SVG files with external DTD references, which, when processed, can cause the application to make arbitrary network requests, leading to Denial of Service (DoS) or Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF).

attack_chain.action: Attacker uploads or submits a crafted SVG file containing an external DTD reference in the DOCTYPE declaration.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application receives and attempts to parse the malicious SVG file.

attack_chain.action: Application parses the SVG file and processes the external DTD, resulting in an HTTP request to the specified host (e.g., localhost:2323).
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential service disruption (DoS) or exposure of internal network resources (SSRF) due to the triggered network request.

behavioral_signatures: SVG file parsing by the application triggers outbound network requests
Detection of external DTD references (<!DOCTYPE ... SYSTEM ...>) in user-supplied SVG files
Unexpected HTTP requests to internal or external hosts during image processing workflows
file_indicators: SVG files containing <!DOCTYPE ... SYSTEM ...> declarations
SVG files referencing non-standard or internal hosts in the DOCTYPE SYSTEM identifier
network_indicators: HTTP requests to arbitrary hosts (e.g., localhost, internal IPs) during SVG file processing
Unusual User-Agent strings (such as Java/1.7.0_60-ea) in requests originating from image parsing services
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan user-supplied SVG files for external DTD references (<!DOCTYPE ... SYSTEM ...>). Monitor for any network activity initiated during SVG parsing, especially HTTP requests to internal or unexpected hosts. Harden XML parsers by disabling external entity resolution for SVG files to prevent XXE exploitation.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when rsh.js is executed as a detached process, the code collects detailed system, environment, and user information, compresses and encodes it, decompresses an obfuscated payload from a base64 string, sets the NODE_NO_EVAL environment variable to undefined, and executes the decompressed payload using eval, resulting in the execution of further malicious code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting extensive system, environment, and user data, compressing and encoding it, and executing obfuscated code via eval are all strong indicators of malicious intent and are commonly used to evade detection and enable data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not collect and exfiltrate system or user information, nor do they execute dynamically decompressed and obfuscated code via eval.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Compression and system info gathering may be used in legitimate diagnostics or telemetry, but not in combination with obfuscated payload execution and without user consent.
key_indicators: Obfuscated and base64-encoded payload decompressed and executed via eval
Systematic collection of system, environment, and user data
Manipulation of environment variables to bypass security controls
No user notification or consent for data collection or code execution

package_info.why_malicious: All packages in this campaign execute obfuscated JavaScript code at install time, which collects extensive system, environment, and user information and establishes a persistent reverse shell to a remote attacker-controlled server (rsh.51pwn.com:8880), enabling full remote code execution and exfiltration of sensitive data. The attack chain is triggered via multiple npm lifecycle hooks, uses detached background processes for persistence, and employs obfuscation and dynamic code execution to evade detection.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed, triggering preinstall, postinstall, test, or init scripts defined in package.json.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of scripts/init.js

attack_chain.action: scripts/init.js is executed, which launches scripts/rsh.js as a detached child process and immediately exits to conceal ongoing activity.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of scripts/rsh.js in the background

attack_chain.action: scripts/rsh.js collects detailed system, environment, and user data, compresses and encodes it, decompresses an obfuscated payload, and executes it via eval.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of reverse shell payload from decompressed code

attack_chain.action: The reverse shell payload establishes a persistent connection to rsh.51pwn.com:8880, exfiltrates collected system information, and provides the attacker with remote shell access for arbitrary command execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent remote access and control over the compromised system

behavioral_signatures: Execution of scripts/init.js during npm install, test, or init lifecycle events
Creation of detached child processes in install/test scripts (child_process.fork with {detached: true})
Presence of obfuscated or base64-encoded JavaScript payloads in package files
Use of eval to execute dynamically decompressed or generated code
Outbound TCP connections to hardcoded C2 domains (e.g., rsh.51pwn.com:8880) during or after installation
Collection and exfiltration of system, environment, and user data during package installation or execution
file_indicators: scripts/init.js
scripts/rsh.js
package.json with install/test/init scripts running 'node ./scripts/init.js'
Obfuscated JavaScript with base64-encoded or Unicode-escaped payloads
network_indicators: rsh.51pwn.com:8880
Outbound TCP connections to rsh.51pwn.com on port 8880
Initial data exfiltration containing compressed system information
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm packages for execution of scripts during install, test, or init lifecycle events, especially those launching detached child processes or containing obfuscated/base64-encoded code. Flag any package that establishes outbound TCP connections to suspicious domains (e.g., rsh.51pwn.com) or uncommon ports during or after installation. Use static analysis to detect eval usage on dynamically decompressed payloads and the presence of Unicode-escaped or base64-encoded code. Alert on collection and exfiltration of system, environment, or user data during package installation or execution. Correlate file indicators (scripts/init.js, scripts/rsh.js, suspicious package.json scripts) with behavioral and network indicators for high-confidence detection.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, on page load or script execution, the code injects external scripts into the page, including a deprecated version of Ionicons and a remote script (slim.js) hosted on jsDelivr, which itself contains the trojanized jQuery. This enables further malicious code execution and persistence by loading additional payloads from attacker-controlled sources.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script injects remote code from attacker-controlled sources without user consent, using a misleading deprecation warning to disguise its activity and facilitate further compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not inject remote scripts or downgrade libraries without explicit user action or clear documentation. Core libraries should not dynamically load external code from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script injection is used in some legitimate plugin loaders, but not in core libraries or without user awareness and explicit opt-in.
key_indicators: Injection of remote scripts from suspicious or attacker-controlled domains
Phony deprecation warnings in console output to mislead users
Use of outdated or deprecated library versions
Chaining to further malicious payloads via dynamic script loading

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, on page load or script execution

package_info.package_versions: 8.0.0 (and dozens of others, see report for full list)
package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a trojanized version of jQuery in which the 'end' prototype function is maliciously modified to exfiltrate all form data from the page to attacker-controlled domains whenever it is called, either directly or indirectly (e.g., via fadeTo). The package is distributed under many names and versions, often with additional suspicious files and unique exfiltration URLs, indicating a persistent, manually assembled supply chain attack targeting web applications.

attack_chain.action: User installs a malicious npm package containing a trojanized jQuery file (or similar).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is present in the project and loaded in the browser.

attack_chain.action: Trojanized jQuery is loaded and used in the web application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious prototype function (end) is available in the global jQuery object.

attack_chain.action: User or application code calls fadeTo or end (directly or indirectly), triggering the malicious end function.
attack_chain.leads_to: Form data is serialized and exfiltrated to attacker-controlled domains.

attack_chain.action: Injected scripts (from icons.js/min.js) load additional remote payloads (e.g., slim.js) from jsDelivr, which may contain further trojanized code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and further compromise of the web application.

behavioral_signatures: Modification of jQuery prototype functions (especially end) to perform network requests
Exfiltration of serialized form data via AJAX to external domains
Dynamic injection of remote scripts from non-standard or outdated sources
Presence of phony deprecation warnings in console output
file_indicators: jquery.min.js, registration.min.js, icon.min.js, fontawesome.js, slim.js, all-min.js (with non-standard or unexpected content)
Presence of termux.properties, npm cache, or npm logs in package tarballs
network_indicators: Requests to domains such as *.truex.biz.id, *.hanznesia.my.id, *.api-system.engineer, *.jsdelivr.net/gh/indexsc/libs/slim.js, and other listed campaign domains
AJAX GET requests with hex-encoded form data in query parameters
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan JavaScript dependencies for modifications to core library prototype functions (e.g., jQuery.fn.end). Flag any code that serializes and exfiltrates form data to external domains. Monitor for dynamic script injection from non-standard or outdated sources, and alert on requests to known campaign domains. Review package contents for unexpected files (e.g., termux.properties, npm logs) and non-standard file naming patterns. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify supply chain attacks.
